A child can eat three times a day and still be malnourished. If every meal is mostly garri, white rice or pap with little beans, fish, egg or vegetables, the stomach is full but the body is missing protein, iron, vitamin A, zinc and iodine. Health workers call this **hidden hunger**. This course is about closing the gap between enough food and the right food, at home and in your community.
A family standing together
Food security is a household and community matter: every member, every season.
What food security means

The definition used by FAO and governments since the 1996 World Food Summit says food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life. That long sentence breaks into four parts, sometimes called the four pillars.
Pillar
Plain question
Local example of a problem
Availability
Is the food there at all?
Tomatoes and leafy vegetables are scarce in the dry season, or a flood destroys the harvest
Access
Can the family get it, with money, farm or gifts?
Beans are in the market but the family cannot afford them this month
Utilisation
Does the body actually use the food well?
Dirty water causes repeated diarrhoea, so the child loses nutrients; or food is overcooked and badly shared
Stability
Is it steady through the year and through shocks?
Food is fine after harvest but runs out between May and August, or prices jump suddenly

Notice that only one pillar is about whether food exists. Many families in Nigerian towns live near busy markets, so availability is fine, yet access is the problem because prices rose faster than income. Utilisation is often forgotten: clean water, handwashing, good cooking and fair sharing inside the home decide whether food becomes nutrition.
The different faces of malnutrition

WHO groups malnutrition into undernutrition, micronutrient problems, and overweight with diet-related diseases. Health workers use three body measures for children under five. Each compares the child with the WHO Child Growth Standards for a healthy child of the same age and sex.

**Stunting**: too short for age. It builds slowly from months of poor diet and repeated illness, often starting in pregnancy. It is linked to poorer learning and is hard to reverse after about age two.
**Wasting**: too thin for height. It can develop quickly after illness or food shortage and is dangerous; severe wasting raises the risk of death and needs urgent treatment.
**Underweight**: low weight for age. It can reflect stunting, wasting or both, and is what the weight line on a child health card shows.
**Micronutrient deficiency**: lack of vitamins and minerals such as iron, vitamin A, iodine and zinc, even when weight looks fine.
**Overweight and obesity**: too much energy, often from sugary drinks, fried snacks and refined starch, which raises the risk of diabetes and high blood pressure later.

One household can carry more than one problem at the same time: a stunted child and an overweight parent eating the same cheap, starchy, oily diet. This is called the **double burden of malnutrition**, and it is why the answer is never just more food. The answer is more variety.
The malnutrition and infection cycle
Poor diet
Weaker immunity
More infections
Less appetite, nutrients lost
Poorer nutrition
Each turn of the cycle makes the next one worse, so breaking it at any point (food, clean water, vaccination, early treatment) helps.

A child with diarrhoea or measles eats less, absorbs less and uses more energy fighting the illness. She comes out of each illness thinner, and a thinner child catches the next infection more easily. That is why community nutrition work always includes clean water, handwashing, immunisation and quick treatment of illness, not only food.
Why the first 1,000 days matter

The period from pregnancy to a child's second birthday is called the **first 1,000 days**. The brain and body grow fastest then, so the effects of good or poor nutrition are largest and longest lasting. A pregnant woman's diet, breastfeeding, and the first foods a baby eats from six months are the most valuable targets for your effort.
Worked example: naming the real problem

For example, Halima in a town near Kano feeds her family of six. They eat tuwo or rice twice a day with a thin soup, and there is enough to feel full. Her 20-month-old son is shorter than his cousins of the same age, and her husband has been told his blood pressure is high.
Availability: food is in the market all year, so this is not the main problem.
Access: she can afford some beans and fish but buys mostly grain because it fills more stomachs per naira.
Utilisation: the soup has little vegetable or protein, and the toddler often has diarrhoea from untreated well water.
Forms of malnutrition: the boy shows signs of stunting; the father's diet is high in salt, oil and refined starch.
Cycle: repeated diarrhoea plus a low-variety diet keeps the boy in the malnutrition and infection cycle.

Halima's household has a double burden and an access plus utilisation problem. Her best first steps are safer drinking water, more beans and leafy vegetables in the soup, and taking the toddler to the clinic for growth measurement, not simply buying more grain.
When to go to a clinic today

A child who is very thin, has swelling of both feet, refuses to eat or drink, is unusually sleepy, or has diarrhoea with signs of dehydration needs a health facility the same day. Food advice is not a substitute for treatment.

In school many of us learned three groups: energy-giving foods, body-building foods and protective foods. That is a good start, but it hides an important point: a meal with rice, a little stew and one slice of tomato ticks all three boxes yet is still poor. Nutrition workers now use a more detailed list of food groups to check whether a diet is varied enough.

The 10 food groups

FAO's Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women (MDD-W) indicator uses 10 groups. A woman who ate foods from at least 5 of the 10 groups yesterday is much more likely to be getting enough vitamins and minerals. We will use the same list for the whole family in this course.

Red palm oil is not one of the 10 groups, because oils are counted separately, but it is worth knowing: unrefined red palm oil is rich in carotenoids that the body turns into vitamin A. Using it in moderation in soups and stews is a traditional strength of many Nigerian diets.
Four nutrients to watch
**Iron** prevents anaemia, which causes tiredness and poor concentration. Best absorbed from liver, meat, fish and crayfish; also found in beans and leafy greens.
**Vitamin A** protects eyesight and helps fight infection. Found in liver, egg yolk, red palm oil, dark green leaves, mango, pawpaw and orange-fleshed sweet potato.
**Iodine** is needed for the brain and thyroid. The simplest source is iodised salt; keep it covered and away from heat so the iodine is not lost.
**Protein** builds and repairs the body. Beans, groundnuts, eggs, fish, milk and meat all provide it, and mixing a grain with a pulse (rice and beans, moi moi with pap) gives better quality protein.
Pair foods to absorb more iron

Vitamin C helps the body absorb the iron in beans and leaves. Eat orange, guava, pawpaw or tomato with the meal. Tea, coffee and some cocoa drinks reduce iron absorption, so take them between meals rather than with food.
Preparation that keeps the goodness

How you prepare food changes what the body receives. Soaking beans overnight and throwing away the soaking water shortens cooking time and makes them easier to digest. Fermenting maize into ogi, or sprouting grains, helps release minerals such as iron and zinc. Leafy vegetables lose vitamin C when boiled for a long time, so add ugu or efo near the end of cooking and cut them just before use rather than hours earlier.
Value for money: cost per gram of protein

When money is tight, compare foods by what they give the body, not by the price per bag. The worked example below uses rough protein values (about 23 g of protein per 100 g of dry beans, about 25 g per 100 g of groundnuts, about 6 g per egg) and example prices. Prices change often, so redo the sums with your own market prices.
Worked example: which protein gives the most for the money?
For example, Ngozi in Enugu has example prices (approximate, check your market): 1 kg of beans for 3,000 naira, 1 kg of groundnuts for 3,200 naira, and a crate of 30 eggs for 7,500 naira.
Beans: 1 kg = 1,000 g, so protein is about 1,000 x 23 / 100 = 230 g. Cost per gram = 3,000 / 230 = about 13 naira.
Groundnuts: protein is about 1,000 x 25 / 100 = 250 g. Cost per gram = 3,200 / 250 = about 12.8 naira.
Eggs: 30 x 6 g = 180 g of protein. Cost per gram = 7,500 / 180 = about 42 naira.
She notes that eggs cost more per gram but give vitamin A, B12 and very high quality protein, and are easy to feed to a baby.

Beans and groundnuts give protein at about one third of the cost of eggs. Ngozi makes beans and groundnut the daily base, and buys a few eggs each week mainly for her one-year-old and her pregnant sister.

Good advice starts with good facts about your own situation. In this lesson you will measure three things: what your household actually ate, how food changes through the year, and what your community already has. Together they become your baseline, the starting point you will compare against at the end of the course.
A person ticking items on a large checklist
A simple food-group tick list turns 'we eat well' into a number you can track.
Tool 1: the 24-hour recall and diversity score
Choose one person (start with yourself or the youngest child above six months).
Ask about everything eaten or drunk from waking yesterday to waking today: meals, snacks, drinks, and food eaten outside the home.
For mixed dishes, list the ingredients. Egusi soup may contain egusi, ugu, palm oil, crayfish and meat.
Tick each of the 10 food groups that appears. Very small amounts used only for flavour, such as a pinch of crayfish powder, are usually not counted.
Count the ticked groups. That number out of 10 is the dietary diversity score. For women, 5 or more is the target.
Worked example: scoring a day

For example, Amina in Ilorin recalls yesterday: pap with sugar in the morning, rice and tomato stew with a small piece of fish at lunch, garri soaked with water and groundnuts in the evening, and one orange.
Pap (maize) and rice and garri: group 1, grains and roots. Tick.
Tomato in the stew: group 9, other vegetables. Tick.
Fish: group 5, meat, poultry and fish. Tick.
Groundnuts: group 3, nuts and seeds. Tick.
Orange: group 10, other fruits. Tick.
No beans, dairy, eggs, leafy greens or vitamin A-rich fruit: groups 2, 4, 6, 7 and 8 missing.
Amina scores 5 out of 10, just at the target, but she has no dark leafy greens or vitamin A-rich foods. Adding ugu to the stew and a slice of ripe pawpaw would lift her to 7 at little cost.

One day can be unusual, so repeat the recall on three different days, including one market day and one non-market day, and take the average. Write the scores down; you will use them again in Module 2.
Tool 2: the seasonal calendar

In much of Nigeria, the months before the main harvest are the hardest. Stored grain runs low, prices rise, and farm work is heavy. Many people call this the lean season or hunger gap. The timing differs by region and by crop, so draw your own calendar instead of copying someone else's.
A seasonal food calendar (fill in your own months)
Harvest: food plentiful, prices low
Dry season: fewer fresh vegetables
Planting: money spent on seeds
Lean months: stores low, prices high
Early harvest: green maize, relief
Mark your own months under each stage, then plan storage and gardens to cover the lean months.

Ask two or three older women in your area to help. For each month, note which foods are cheap, which are scarce, when school fees or farm costs fall, and when illnesses such as malaria and diarrhoea are common. Problems that pile up in the same months show you where to act first.
Tool 3: the community food map
Food sources: markets, shops, farms, fishing points, and where people buy cooked food.
Water sources: which are protected (borehole, treated tap) and which are not (open well, stream).
Health support: the nearest primary health care centre, its immunisation and growth monitoring days, and community health workers.
Farming support: agricultural extension officers, cooperatives, and seed or seedling sellers.
Groups: women's associations, religious groups, savings groups and school PTAs that could carry a nutrition message.

If you can only change one thing in your community, change how babies and young children are fed. WHO and UNICEF guidance, followed by Nigeria's Federal Ministry of Health, is clear and simple. This lesson turns it into practical steps with local foods.
A mother holding her baby
Breastfeeding and good first foods are the strongest protection in the first 1,000 days.
Birth to six months: breast milk only
Put the baby to the breast within **one hour of birth**. The first thick yellow milk, colostrum, is rich in antibodies; do not throw it away.

Give **only breast milk for the first six months**: no water, glucose water, herbal drinks, pap or formula unless a health worker advises it for a medical reason. Breast milk contains enough water even in hot weather.
Feed on demand, day and night. Frequent feeding keeps the milk supply up.
Continue breastfeeding **up to two years or beyond** while other foods are added.
From six months: first foods

At about six months, breast milk alone no longer covers a baby's needs for energy, iron and zinc. WHO advises starting small amounts of food and increasing gradually: 2 to 3 meals a day at 6 to 8 months, and 3 to 4 meals a day at 9 to 23 months, with 1 to 2 nutritious snacks if the child is hungry. The table uses a 250 ml cup, about the size of a standard plastic drinking cup.

Variety: at least 5 of 8 groups

For children aged 6 to 23 months, WHO and UNICEF measure **minimum dietary diversity** with 8 groups: breast milk; grains, roots, tubers and plantain; pulses, nuts and seeds; dairy; flesh foods (meat, fish, poultry, liver); eggs; vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables; and other fruits and vegetables. A child who ate from at least 5 of these 8 groups yesterday meets the target. Plain pap made from maize or millet alone covers only one group, which is why it must be enriched.
Worked example: enriching ogi for an 8-month-old
For example, Chiamaka in Owerri gives her 8-month-old daughter plain ogi with a little sugar twice a day, plus breast milk. The baby's diet scores 2 of 8 (breast milk and grains).
She makes the ogi thicker so it stays on a tilted spoon, instead of a thin drink.
Into about half a 250 ml cup of ogi she stirs 1 tablespoon of smooth groundnut paste (pulses, nuts and seeds).
She adds 1 teaspoon of finely ground crayfish, checked for grit and sand (flesh foods).
At lunch she mashes a soft-boiled egg into yam or rice (eggs), and gives mashed ripe pawpaw as a snack (vitamin A-rich fruit).
She drops the added sugar, since the groundnut and fruit already make the food tasty.
The baby now eats from breast milk, grains, nuts, flesh foods, eggs and vitamin A-rich fruit: 6 of 8 groups, above the target, at a modest extra cost.
Baby food safety

Wash hands with soap before preparing food and before feeding. Use a clean cup and spoon, not a feeding bottle, which is hard to clean. Grind groundnuts into smooth paste, because whole nuts can choke a young child. Do not give honey before the first birthday. Avoid sweet drinks, tea and coffee for young children, and feed freshly made food rather than food kept for hours.
Responsive feeding and the sick child

Sit with the child, talk to her, and watch for signs of hunger and fullness. Encourage, but never force or threaten. Give the child her own plate so you can see how much she ate. When a child is ill, keep breastfeeding and offer small, frequent meals and fluids; after the illness, offer more food than usual for some time to help her catch up. Children with diarrhoea should be taken to a health worker for oral rehydration salts and zinc as advised.
Mothers need extra food too

Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more energy and nutrients. WHO and UNICEF counselling materials commonly advise about one extra small meal or snack a day during pregnancy and two while breastfeeding, from varied foods. Pregnant women should attend antenatal care early, where the clinic provides iron and folic acid supplements; take them exactly as the health worker directs. Use iodised salt, and make sure the mother is not the one who always eats last and least.

Food that is contaminated, mouldy or badly shared does not become good nutrition. This lesson covers the utilisation pillar: keeping food safe from farm to plate and making sure the people who need it most actually get it.
A person washing hands at a sink
Washing hands with soap and safe water is the first of the WHO Five Keys.
The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
These five habits prevent most foodborne illness in homes and food businesses.
**Keep clean**: wash hands with soap before handling food and after using the toilet or changing a nappy; keep surfaces, pots and cloths clean; cover food from flies.
**Separate raw and cooked**: keep raw meat, fish and their juices away from cooked food and fruit; use a separate knife and board, or wash them well between uses.
**Cook thoroughly**: cook meat, chicken, eggs and fish until juices run clear and there is no pink; bring soups and stews to the boil when reheating.
**Keep food at safe temperatures**: do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours; keep it hot (above 60 degrees C) or cold (below 5 degrees C); reheat until steaming hot.
**Use safe water and raw materials**: use boiled or treated water; choose fresh, undamaged food; wash fruits and vegetables, especially if eaten raw; do not use food after its expiry date.
Worked example: leftovers after a naming ceremony
For example, Ruth in Ibadan cooked jollof rice and chicken stew that were ready at 1 pm. Guests left at 5 pm. She has no fridge, but there is light most evenings at her neighbour's house.
Time at room temperature: from 1 pm to 5 pm is 4 hours, double the 2-hour limit.
The rice has been sitting warm for 4 hours. Cooked rice left warm can grow bacteria whose toxins are not destroyed by reheating, so she does not keep it for the children.
For the next event she plans ahead: she will keep stew in the pot on a low fire, above 60 degrees C, and serve rice in batches.
Any portion she wants to keep will be cooled in shallow bowls and taken to the neighbour's fridge within 2 hours of cooking.
Kept stew will be boiled again until it bubbles before eating the next day.
Ruth throws away the rice left out for 4 hours instead of risking diarrhoea in her children, and writes a simple plan so that next time no food sits out beyond 2 hours.
Safe drinking water at home

Water from open wells, streams and some boreholes can carry germs that cause diarrhoea, which steals nutrients from children. If you are not sure your water is safe, bring it to a rolling boil, let it cool covered, and store it in a clean container with a lid and a tap, or pour it out rather than dipping cups and hands inside. Water for preparing baby food and mixing oral rehydration salts must always be safe water.
Storing grain, beans and groundnuts

Moulds that grow on damp or damaged maize, groundnuts and other grains can produce **aflatoxins**, poisons that you cannot see, smell or cook away. Long-term exposure is linked to liver damage, and in children to poor growth. Prevention is all about dryness and sorting.

Dry grain and legumes well before storing. A simple check: put a handful of grain and two spoons of dry salt in a dry, clear bottle, close and shake for a minute. If salt sticks to the sides, the grain is still too damp.
Sort and remove mouldy, shrivelled, discoloured or insect-damaged grains and nuts. Throw them away; do not sell them or feed them to animals.
Store in clean, airtight containers or hermetic (airtight) storage bags, such as triple-layer PICS bags widely used for cowpeas. Without air, weevils die without chemicals.
Keep sacks off the floor on wooden pallets and away from walls, in a dry, cool, ventilated place.
Never store food in containers that held fuel, pesticide or chemicals, and never mix storage chemicals into food meant for home use.
Fair sharing inside the home

In many homes the best pieces of meat or fish go to the father or to guests, and young children eat from a shared bowl with older siblings who eat faster. These customs come from respect and love, but they can leave the people with the highest needs short. A family may feel it is eating better, but feelings can mislead. Health workers rely on a few simple measures. You do not need to diagnose anyone: your role is to keep good records, notice warning signs early, and connect families to the clinic.
A rising growth chart
A child's weight line should keep rising in the same direction as the printed curves.
Measure 1: the growth line on the child health card

At immunisation and growth monitoring sessions, clinics weigh children and plot the weight on a chart on the child health card, based on the WHO Child Growth Standards. Read the **direction of the line**, not just one dot. A line rising alongside the printed curves is good. A flat line between two visits, or a line going down, means the child is not growing as expected and needs a health worker's attention and a feeding check, even if the child looks fine. Take the card to every visit and ask the nurse to explain it.
Measure 2: MUAC and the oedema check

MUAC means **mid-upper arm circumference**. A coloured MUAC tape is wrapped around the left upper arm, halfway between the shoulder tip and the elbow, with the arm hanging relaxed. It is used for children aged 6 to 59 months, and many programmes now train mothers to use it themselves. The cut-offs below come from the WHO and UNICEF joint statement on severe acute malnutrition.

Meaning

Also check for **bilateral pitting oedema**: press your thumbs gently on the top of both feet for 3 seconds. If a dent remains on both feet after you lift your thumbs, the child has oedema, which is a sign of severe acute malnutrition whatever the MUAC reading. Refer at once. In Nigeria, community management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) sites at primary health care centres treat these children, often as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food.

Screening only helps when every red, yellow or oedema result leads to a clinic visit and a follow-up.
Your role is to refer, not treat

Never give medicines, supplements or therapeutic food on your own, and never tell a family a child is fine because the tape is green if the child looks very ill. Danger signs such as not able to drink, repeated vomiting, convulsions or unusual sleepiness need a health facility immediately.
Worked example: a yellow MUAC result
For example, Fatima, a volunteer in a Zaria women's group, has been trained by the community health worker to use a MUAC tape. She measures 18-month-old Sani's arm at 118 mm and finds no oedema.
118 mm is between 115 and 124 mm, so the tape shows yellow: moderate acute malnutrition.
She explains calmly to Sani's mother what yellow means and that the clinic can help.
She writes the date, child number, reading (118 mm), oedema (none) and action (referred) in her register.
She agrees with the mother to go to the clinic on its next nutrition day, three days later, and offers to go along.
Two weeks later she visits again and records the new reading.
Sani is assessed and enrolled for feeding support. Fatima's record shows the referral, the visit, and the follow-up reading, so nobody is lost between screening and care.
Measure 3: the weekly diet diversity tracker

For household change, keep a 7-day tracker. Each evening, score the day out of 10 groups for yourself (or out of 8 for a young child). At the end of each week calculate two numbers: the **average score** (total divided by 7) and the **percentage of days that reached the target** (days at 5 or more divided by 7, times 100).
Worked example: four weeks of tracking
For example, Amina from Module 1 started adding ugu, beans and pawpaw. Her daily scores in week 1 were 4, 3, 5, 4, 4, 3, 5. In week 4 they were 6, 5, 5, 6, 7, 5, 6.
Week 1 days at 5 or more: 2. Percentage = 2 / 7 x 100 = about 29%.
Week 4 total: 6 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 5 + 6 = 40. Average = 40 / 7 = about 5.7.
Week 4 days at 5 or more: 7. Percentage = 7 / 7 x 100 = 100%.
Amina's average rose from 4.0 to 5.7 and she now reaches the target every day. Continuing to track past week 4 will show whether the change lasts through the lean season.

Setting up a sack garden
Choose a sunny spot near the kitchen door that gets at least half a day of sun and is safe from goats and chickens.
Use strong woven sacks or old buckets with holes punched in the bottom for drainage.
Fill with a mix of good topsoil and well-rotted manure or compost. Put a column of small stones down the middle of large sacks to help water reach the roots.
Plant leafy greens on top and in slits on the sides: efo tete from seed, ugu from its large seeds, waterleaf from stem cuttings.
Water early morning or evening. Rinse water from washing vegetables or rice can be reused, but avoid water with heavy soap or bleach.
Harvest outer leaves regularly so the plant keeps producing; replant a sack every few months.
Get local advice
Your state Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension officer, a nearby farmer or a seed seller can tell you which varieties do best in your area and season. Ask before buying seed.
Worked example: does a garden pay?

For example, Kemi in Abeokuta buys a bundle of ugu three times a week for about 500 naira each (approximate). Setup costs (approximate): 4 sacks at 300 naira, topsoil and manure 3,000 naira, seeds and cuttings 2,000 naira.
Current spending on ugu: 3 x 500 = 1,500 naira per week.
Once the sacks are producing enough, the saving is about 1,500 naira per week.
Payback time: 6,200 / 1,500 = about 4 weeks of harvesting.
She also gains fresher leaves picked minutes before cooking, which keeps more vitamin C.
After the first harvests, Kemi's garden pays for itself in about a month and then saves her roughly 6,000 naira a month at these example prices, money she moves to eggs for her toddler.
Eggs from a few hens

A few local hens kept for eggs can give young children a regular source of high quality protein and vitamin A. Eggs are worth more on the child's plate than sold, if the family can manage it. Keep hens in a coop or run, away from the kitchen and the place where babies crawl and play, because contact with animal droppings spreads germs that cause diarrhoea. Wash hands after handling birds or collecting eggs, and cook eggs until the white and yolk are firm.

Ask specifically

For example, Grace leads a women's fellowship of 30 members in Makurdi. Her baseline shows 14 children under five in members' homes, and only 4 have been weighed in the last three months.

Protect privacy: never post a child's MUAC result, photo or name in a group without the parent's clear permission.

Invite fathers to a short session at a men's meeting or after prayers, focused on what they can do: give money for eggs and beans, build the garden or coop, and support exclusive breastfeeding. Invite grandmothers to the cooking demonstration and ask for their experience before sharing new advice.

Module 1 video
Full stomach, hidden hunger: seeing the real food problem
Full stomach, hidden hunger: seeing the real food problem.
This is the video for module one of Community Nutrition and Food Security.
Why this matters
Enough food is not the right food
Garri, rice or pap at every meal
Stomach full, body still missing nutrients
This is called hidden hunger
The answer is more variety
A child can eat three times a day and still be malnourished. If every meal is mostly garri, white rice or pap, the stomach is full but the body is missing protein, iron, vitamin A, zinc and iodine.
Health workers call this hidden hunger.
This module helps you see the real problem in your home and community. And the answer is never just more food. It is more variety.
Food security
The four pillars
Availability: is the food there at all?
Access: can the family get it?
Utilisation: does the body use it well?
Stability: is it steady all year?
Food security has four parts. Availability asks: is the food there at all? For example, vegetables are scarce in the dry season.
Access asks: can the family get it? Beans may be in the market, but the family cannot afford them this month.
Utilisation is often forgotten. Dirty water causes repeated diarrhoea, so the child loses nutrients. Clean water, handwashing and fair sharing decide whether food becomes nutrition.
Stability asks: does food last through the year and through shocks, like sudden price jumps?
Know the signs
Faces of malnutrition
Too short for age. Builds slowly from poor diet and repeated illness. Hard to reverse after about age two.
Too thin for height. Can develop quickly after illness or food shortage, and is dangerous.
Lack of iron, vitamin A, iodine or zinc, even when weight looks fine.

Stunting means too short for age. It builds slowly from months of poor diet and illness, and is hard to reverse after about age two. That is why the first 1,000 days, from pregnancy to age two, matter most.
Wasting means too thin for height. It can come quickly after illness or food shortage, and severe wasting needs urgent treatment.
Micronutrient deficiency, or hidden hunger, can be there even when weight looks fine.
Poor diet and infection feed each other in a cycle. So water, hygiene, vaccination and quick treatment are part of nutrition too.
Safety first
Go to a clinic the same day if
The child is very thin
Both feet are swollen
Refuses to eat or drink
Unusually sleepy
Diarrhoea with signs of dehydration

Know these danger signs. A child who is very thin, has swelling of both feet, refuses to eat or drink, is unusually sleepy, or has diarrhoea with signs of dehydration needs a health facility the same day.
Food advice is not a substitute for treatment.
Worked example
Cost per gram of protein
For example, Ngozi in Enugu compares beans, groundnuts and a crate of eggs at her market.
Beans, per gram of protein
Groundnuts, per gram of protein
Eggs, per gram of protein
Example naira prices; check your own market.
When money is tight, compare foods by what they give the body, not by the price per bag.
Ngozi's example prices are 3,000 naira for 1 kg of beans, 3,200 for 1 kg of groundnuts, and 7,500 for a crate of 30 eggs. Prices change, so use your own.
Beans give about 230 g of protein, so each gram costs about 13 naira. Groundnuts come to about 12.8 naira.
Eggs cost about 42 naira per gram. But eggs give vitamin A and very high quality protein, and are easy to feed a baby.
So Ngozi makes beans and groundnuts the daily base, and buys a few eggs for her one-year-old and her pregnant sister.
Measure it
Your dietary diversity score
Recall everything eaten from waking yesterday
List the ingredients of mixed dishes
Tick each of the 10 food groups present
Count the ticks: your score out of 10
Repeat on three days and average
For women, 5 or more food groups is the target.
Now measure your starting point. Ask about everything eaten or drunk from waking yesterday to waking today, including snacks and food eaten outside.

Tick each of the 10 food groups that appears, like grains, pulses, eggs, dark green leaves and vitamin A-rich fruits. A pinch used only for flavour usually does not count. The number of ticks is the score.
One day can be unusual, so repeat on three different days and take the average.
For example, Amina scored 5 out of 10, just at the target. Adding ugu to her stew and a slice of ripe pawpaw would lift her to 7 at little cost.
Get more from food
Small habits, big gains
Eat vitamin C foods with beans and leaves
Keep tea and coffee away from meals
Add ugu or efo near the end of cooking
Use iodised salt, kept covered
Cut sugary drinks first
Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from beans and leaves, so eat orange, guava or tomato with the meal. Take tea and coffee between meals.
Add leafy vegetables near the end of cooking, because long boiling loses vitamin C. Keep iodised salt covered and away from heat.
And sugary drinks and packaged snacks eat a surprising share of the budget. Cut them first to pay for beans and leaves.
Key points
Remember
Four pillars: availability, access, utilisation, stability
Stunting, wasting and hidden hunger
Danger signs need a clinic the same day
Compare protein by cost per gram
Aim for 5 or more food groups a day
To remember. Food security has four pillars. Malnutrition has many faces, and danger signs need a clinic the same day.
Compare protein foods by cost per gram, and aim for at least 5 food groups a day.

Feeding, food safety and measuring change in the field
Feeding, food safety and measuring change.
This is the video for module two of Community Nutrition and Food Security.
Why this matters
If you change one thing
Feed babies and young children well
Keep food safe from farm to plate
Measure, record and refer early
If you can only change one thing in your community, change how babies and young children are fed. WHO and UNICEF guidance is clear and simple.
This module gives you three practical tools: feeding the first 1,000 days, keeping food safe, and simple measures of progress.
Birth to six months
Breast milk first, breast milk only
Breastfeed within one hour of birth
Keep the colostrum, do not throw it away
Only breast milk for six months
Feed on demand, day and night
Continue up to two years or beyond
Put the baby to the breast within one hour of birth. The first thick yellow milk, colostrum, is rich in antibodies. Do not throw it away.
Give only breast milk for the first six months. No water, herbal drinks or pap, unless a health worker advises it for a medical reason. Breast milk contains enough water even in hot weather.
Feed on demand, day and night, and continue breastfeeding up to two years or beyond while other foods are added.
From six months
First foods, step by step
6 to 8 months: thick, mashed food
2 to 3 meals a day, plus breastfeeds
9 to 23 months: 3 to 4 meals
Add 1 to 2 snacks if hungry
Aim for 5 of 8 food groups
Thick enough to stay on a tilted spoon, never a thin drink.
At about six months, breast milk alone no longer covers a baby's needs for energy, iron and zinc. Start with thick porridge or well-mashed food.
At 6 to 8 months, give 2 to 3 meals a day, starting with 2 to 3 tablespoons and slowly increasing.
From 9 to 23 months, give 3 to 4 meals a day, with 1 to 2 nutritious snacks if the child is hungry.
For variety, aim for at least 5 of the 8 food groups for young children. Plain pap covers only one group, so it must be enriched.
Worked example
Chiamaka enriches her baby's ogi
Before: 2 of 8
Thin ogi with sugar
Breast milk
Grains only
After: 6 of 8
Thicker ogi, no added sugar
Smooth groundnut paste
Ground crayfish, checked for grit
Mashed egg, ripe pawpaw
For example, Chiamaka in Owerri gave her 8-month-old daughter thin ogi with sugar, plus breast milk. That scores just 2 of 8 groups.
She made the ogi thicker and stirred in 1 tablespoon of smooth groundnut paste and 1 teaspoon of ground crayfish.
At lunch she mashed an egg into yam, and gave ripe pawpaw as a snack. She dropped the sugar. Now the baby eats from 6 of 8 groups, at a modest extra cost.
Safety first
Wash hands with soap. Use a clean cup and spoon, not a feeding bottle.
Grind groundnuts into smooth paste. Whole nuts can choke a young child.
No honey before the first birthday. No sweet drinks, tea or coffee. Feed fresh food.
Keep baby food safe. Wash hands with soap before preparing food and before feeding. Use a clean cup and spoon, because a feeding bottle is hard to clean.
Grind groundnuts into smooth paste, because whole nuts can choke a young child.
Do not give honey before the first birthday. Avoid sweet drinks, tea and coffee, and feed freshly made food, not food kept for hours.
Safe food at home
Dry and sort grain; throw out mould

Food that is contaminated or mouldy does not become good nutrition. Follow the five keys. Keep clean. Separate raw and cooked. Cook thoroughly. Keep food at safe temperatures. And use safe, boiled or treated water.
Dry grain and groundnuts well, and throw away mouldy ones. The poison in mould cannot be seen or cooked away.
Leftovers
Ruth and the 2-hour rule
Rice ready at 1 pm, guests gone at 5 pm
That is 4 hours: double the limit
She throws the rice away
Next time: stew hot, rice in batches
Cooked food: no more than 2 hours at room temperature.
For example, Ruth in Ibadan cooked jollof rice and stew for a naming ceremony. It was ready at 1 pm, and guests left at 5 pm. She has no fridge.
That is 4 hours at room temperature, double the 2-hour limit. Rice left warm can grow bacteria whose poisons reheating does not destroy.
So she throws the rice away instead of risking diarrhoea in her children.
Next time she will keep stew on a low fire, serve rice in batches, and take food to keep to her neighbour's fridge within 2 hours.
Measure it
Reading a MUAC tape
Severe acute malnutrition. Refer to a health facility the same day.
Moderate acute malnutrition. Clinic assessment and feeding support.
Not acutely malnourished by MUAC. Keep feeding well; recheck monthly.
MUAC means mid-upper arm circumference, for children aged 6 to 59 months. Red means severe acute malnutrition. Refer the same day.
Also press both feet for 3 seconds. A dent left on both feet is oedema, which also means refer at once.
Yellow means moderate acute malnutrition. Fatima measured 18-month-old Sani at 118 mm, explained calmly, went with his mother to the clinic, and recorded a follow-up reading.
Green means keep feeding well and recheck monthly. Your role is to screen, record and refer. Never give medicines or therapeutic food yourself.
Key points
Remember
Breastfeed within one hour, only breast milk to six months
Thick, enriched first foods; 5 of 8 groups
No cooked food out more than 2 hours
Red MUAC or oedema: same-day referral
Track the weekly diet score and its average
To remember. Breastfeed early and exclusively for six months, then add thick, enriched foods.
Keep cooked food out no more than 2 hours. Refer red MUAC or oedema the same day. And track your weekly diet score.

From your pot to your community: gardens, partners and a 90-day plan
From your pot to your community: gardens, partners and a 90-day plan.
This is the video for module three of Community Nutrition and Food Security.
Why this matters
Knowledge must change the pot
Take the gap you found in Module 1
Choose one change that closes it
Start small and make it a habit
Then spread it with partners
Knowledge only helps when it changes the pot. In module one you wrote one specific gap. Now choose one practical change that closes it.
Start small and make it a habit. One change that lasts beats five changes that stop after a fortnight. Then spread it, with partners.
Step by step
Set up a sack garden
A sunny spot, safe from goats and chickens
Strong sacks with drainage holes
Topsoil mixed with rotted manure
Plant greens on top and in side slits
Harvest outer leaves regularly
Do not water with rinse water that has heavy soap or bleach.
If your gap is few dark green leaves, grow them by the kitchen door, in a sunny spot safe from goats and chickens.
Use strong woven sacks or old buckets with holes in the bottom. Fill with good topsoil and well-rotted manure or compost.
Plant on top and in side slits: efo tete from seed, ugu from its large seeds, waterleaf from cuttings. Water early morning or evening.
Harvest the outer leaves regularly so the plant keeps producing.
Rinse water from washing vegetables or rice can be reused, but avoid water with heavy soap or bleach.
Worked example
Does a garden pay?
For example, Kemi in Abeokuta buys ugu three times a week, about 500 naira a bundle.
4 sacks at 300 each
Topsoil and manure
Seeds and cuttings
Naira prices are approximate examples.
Kemi spends about 1,500 naira a week on ugu. Can a garden save money?
She buys 4 sacks at 300 naira each, topsoil and manure for 3,000, and seeds and cuttings for 2,000.
The setup is about 6,200 naira. Once the sacks are producing, she saves about 1,500 naira a week, so the garden pays for itself in about 4 weeks.
She moves the saving to eggs for her toddler. And her leaves are picked minutes before cooking, which keeps more vitamin C.
Safety first
Eggs from a few hens, safely
Use a coop or run, away from the kitchen and where babies crawl and play.
Wash hands after handling birds or collecting eggs. Droppings spread diarrhoea germs.
Cook eggs until the white and the yolk are firm. Eggs are worth more on the child's plate.
A few local hens can give young children regular eggs. Keep them in a coop or run, away from the kitchen and from where babies crawl.
Wash hands after handling birds or collecting eggs, because contact with droppings spreads germs that cause diarrhoea.
Cook eggs until the white and yolk are firm. If the family can manage it, eggs are worth more on the child's plate than sold.
Partners
Clinic and community health workers
ADP agricultural extension officers
Women's, religious and savings groups
One household can change its own pot. A group of households working with partners can change a community.
The primary health care centre offers growth monitoring, MUAC screening, antenatal care and referral.
The Ward Development Committee links you to the health facility. Agricultural extension officers advise on seeds, small livestock and storage.
And your women's, religious and savings groups give you regular meetings and trusted voices. Bring fathers and grandmothers in too.
Grace's request to the clinic
Visit and ask for the officer in charge
Share your baseline numbers
Ask for one specific thing, with a date
Offer what your group will do
Confirm in writing the same day
Partners respond to clear requests. For example, Grace leads a fellowship in Makurdi. She visited the clinic and asked for the officer in charge.
She explained: our members have 14 children under five, and only 4 were weighed in the last three months.
She asked for growth monitoring and MUAC screening at the hall on one Sunday, and offered the space and to bring all 14 children with their cards.
She confirmed the date on WhatsApp that day. All 14 children were measured, and 2 were referred.
Cooking demonstration
Sharing the cost of a demo
For example, a group plans a cooking demonstration for 15 mothers and caregivers.
Ingredients
Firewood or gas
Naira prices are approximate.
Cooking and tasting together changes what families eat. Pick one recipe that fixes your gap, such as enriched pap, and ask a health worker to co-lead.
Set up a handwashing point with soap and safe water, and follow the five keys in front of everyone.
Ingredients of about 9,000 naira plus 1,000 for fuel makes 10,000 naira, about 670 naira each for 15 people.
Follow up a week later: who cooked it, and what was hard?
Your project
Measure, prove, plan
Re-measure with exactly the same tools
Prove it lasts: dated photos, trackers
Write SMART goals for 90 days
Share results in five minutes
If a number did not improve, say so and explain why.
Finally, compare before and after using exactly the same measures, like your 3-day average diversity score.
Show the change lasts, with dated garden photos and several weeks of ticked meal plans and trackers.
Then write SMART goals: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. For example, Bisi's 6 neighbouring households average 3.9. Her goal is 5.0 by day 90.
Present the results honestly. A modest real improvement is worth more than an impressive claim nobody can check.
Key points
Remember
One change that closes your gap
Sack gardens can pay for themselves
Keep hens away from kitchen and babies
Make specific requests with your numbers
SMART goals, same measures, honest reports
To remember. Choose one change that closes your gap, and cost it. Keep hens away from the kitchen and babies.
Ask partners for specific help, backed by your baseline. And measure with the same tools, set SMART goals, and report honestly.
